reasoning:
The two submissions are byte-for-byte identical in executable code. Both change exactly one instruction in `clrCastleSq`: `and 0xFE` -> `and 0xFD` in the `cp 0x00` (a1) branch. Every other added line in both diffs is a comment. Any score gap between them would therefore be manufactured, so I am scoring them equal and calling it a tie; the rubric's instruction to discriminate does not apply when the changes really are equivalent.

CORRECTNESS (5 both). The fix is root-cause and verifiable from inside the hunk itself. The report states h1/a8/h8 behave correctly, and those three untouched branches mask with 0xFE (clears bit0), 0xF7 (bit3) and 0xFB (bit2) for h1/a8/h8 -- which pins the encoding as 0=WK, 1=WQ, 2=BK, 3=BQ and shows bit1 (WQ, a1) was the one right nothing ever cleared. The a1 branch was clearing 0xFE, i.e. the KINGSIDE bit: precisely the reported symptom pair (queenside survives `Ra1-a2`, kingside is revoked instead, repro 3). 0xFD = 11111101 clears bit1 and nothing else, so the change is exactly the correction required and cannot disturb the other three corners, whose masks are untouched.

It also accounts for the headline symptom, not just the two castling-right ones. With WQ still set after Ra1-a2, White's O-O-O remains in the generated move list; when Black's reply drives the engine's reply generation (check/mate/stalemate scan -- the repro uses --two-player so no search runs, but legality/terminal detection still generates), make-castle writes a rook to d1 and unmake writes one back to a1 unconditionally, manufacturing a piece that was never there and taking Matl 5 -> 10. That matches the report's own "castling must never change the material on the board" expectation and matches the timing ("the extra rook arrives with Black's reply"). Revoking the right at source removes the illegal generation, so the phantom rook, repro 2, repro 3 and the Kiwipete depth-3 delta all resolve from the same one-bit repair. I note this last link is inferred from the report rather than shown, and neither submission includes any test evidence; the make/unmake asymmetry also remains latent for any future path that offers castling without a rook home. That residual is identical for both and is not what the defect asked to be fixed, so it does not separate them.

MINIMALITY (5 both). One instruction changed, in the one branch the report isolates. Neither submission touched the other three corner branches, the callers, or the make/unmake path -- the correct call, since hardening make/unmake would be scope the report does not require once rights are accurate.

CLARITY (5 both). Both add a two-line header plus four per-branch annotations spelling out the bit assignment, which is what makes the change reviewable: in the original, `and 0xFE` next to `cp 0x00` carries no way to tell right from wrong. The wording differs and the emphasis differs -- X documents the register contract (A=square, B=rights) and says "from or to a corner square", so a reviewer can verify the `cp`/`ld a,b`/`and`/`ld b,a` idiom without leaving the file; Y documents the rationale ("a rook leaving or being captured") and cross-references chess.asm as the definition site for the bit numbering, giving provenance for the load-bearing claim instead of asserting it. X's assertion is independently corroborated by the three unchanged masks in the same hunk, so Y's pointer buys little that the diff does not already show; conversely Y's rationale line explains why a capture on a corner must also clear the right. These are complementary strengths of roughly equal value, not a ranking.

MERGE: either -- merging X or Y produces the identical binary. If forced to pick on documentation alone I would take X's header for the explicit register contract and fold Y's "see chess.asm" pointer into it, but that is an editorial preference, not a review finding.

BLINDING NOTE: I formed no theory about authorship and could not have -- the two diffs are indistinguishable apart from comment prose, and the comment styles do not favour any particular hypothesis. Scored purely on the code.
